exampleAnswers.title: Finding a Horizontal Asymptote When the Degrees of the Numerator and Denominator are Equal

question.text: Determine the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x) = \dfrac{9-x^3}{2x^3+x}.$
question.explanation:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to\infty.$

In this case, the dominant term in the denominator is $x^3.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by $x^3,$ as follows:

\begin{align} f(x) &=\frac{9-x^3}{2x^3+x}\\[5pt] & = \frac{\left( \dfrac{9}{x^3} - \dfrac{x^3}{x^3}\right)}{\left( \dfrac{2x^3}{x^3} + \dfrac{x}{x^3}\right)}\\[5pt] & = \frac{\left(\dfrac{9}{x^3}-1\right)}{\left(2 + \dfrac{1}{x^2}\right)} \end{align}

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\dfrac{9}{x^3}$ and $\dfrac{1}{x^2}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x \to \infty,$ we have

\begin{align} f(x) & = \frac{\left(\dfrac{9}{x^3}-1\right)}{\left(2 + \dfrac{1}{x^2}\right)}\\[5pt] & \to \dfrac{0-1}{2+0}\\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{1}{2}. \end{align}

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y = -\dfrac{1}{2}.$

question.text: Determine the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x) = \dfrac{2x^4+3x^3}{16x^4-1}.$
question.explanation:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to\infty.$

In this case, the dominant term in the denominator is $x^4.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by $x^4,$ as follows:

\begin{align} f(x) &=\frac{2x^4+3x^3}{16x^4-1}\\[5pt] & = \frac{\left(\dfrac{2x^4}{x^4} + \dfrac{3x^3}{x^4}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{16x^4}{x^4} - \dfrac{1}{x^4}\right)}\\[5pt] & = \frac{\left( 2 + \dfrac{3}{x}\right)}{\left(16 - \dfrac{1}{x^4}\right)} \end{align}

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\dfrac{3}{x}$ and $\dfrac{1}{x^4}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to\infty,$ we have

\begin{align} f(x) & = \frac{\left( 2 + \dfrac{3}{x}\right)}{\left(16 - \dfrac{1}{x^4}\right)}\\[5pt] & \to \dfrac{2+0}{16-0}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{8}. \end{align}

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y=\dfrac{1}{8}.$

question.text: Determine the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x) = \dfrac{7x^2+4}{x(3x^2+12)}.$
question.explanation:
The given function can be rewritten as follows: \[ f(x) = \dfrac{7x^2+4}{3x^3+12x} \]

To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to\infty.$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is $x^3.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by $x^3,$ as follows:

\begin{align} f(x) &= \dfrac{7x^2+4}{3x^3+12x}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{7x^2}{x^3} + \dfrac{4}{x^3}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{3x^3}{x^3}+\dfrac{12x}{x^3}\right)}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{7}{x} + \dfrac{4}{x^3}\right)}{\left(3 + \dfrac{12}{x^2}\right)} \end{align}

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\dfrac{7}{x}, \dfrac{4}{x^3}$ and $\dfrac{12}{x^2}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to\infty,$ we have

\begin{align} f(x) & = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{7}{x} + \dfrac{4}{x^3}\right)}{\left(3 + \dfrac{12}{x^2}\right)}\\[5pt] & \to \dfrac{0+0}{3+0}\\[5pt] & = 0. \end{align}

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y=0.$

question.text: Determine the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x) =\dfrac{x+2}{x^2-9}.$
question.explanation:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to\infty.$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is $x^2.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by $x^2,$ as follows:

\begin{align} f(x) & = \dfrac { x + 2}{x^2-9}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{x}{x^2} + \dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{x^2}{x^2} - \dfrac{9}{x^2} \right)}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{1}{x} + \dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)}{\left(1 - \dfrac{9}{x^2}\right)} \end{align}

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\dfrac{1}{x}, \dfrac{2}{x^2}$ and $\dfrac{9}{x^2}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to\infty,$ we have

\begin{align} f(x) & = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{1}{x} + \dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)}{\left(1 - \dfrac{9}{x^2}\right)}\\[5pt] & \to \dfrac{0+0}{1-0 }\\[5pt] & = 0. \end{align}

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y=0.$

exampleAnswers.title: Finding a Horizontal Asymptote When the Degree of the Numerator is Greater

question.explanation:
The given function can be rewritten as follows:

\[ f(x) = \dfrac{10-3x-x^2}{17x+7} \]

To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to\infty.$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is $x.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by $x,$ as follows:

\begin{align} f(x) &= \dfrac{10-3x-x^2}{17x+7}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\left( \dfrac{10}{x} - \dfrac{3x}{x} - \dfrac{x^2}{x}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{17x}{x} + \dfrac{7}{x}\right)}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{10}{x} -3- x\right)}{\left(17 + \dfrac{7}{x}\right)}\\[5pt] %& = \left(\dfrac{x\left[\dfrac{10}{x^2} -\dfrac{3}{x}- 1\right]}{17+\dfrac{7}{x}}\right)\,. \end{align}

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\dfrac{10}{x}$ and $\dfrac{7}{x}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to\infty,$ we have

\begin{align} f(x) & = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{10}{x} -3- x\right)}{\left(17 + \dfrac{7}{x}\right)}\\[5pt] & \approx \dfrac{0 - 3 - x}{17 + 0}\\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{x + 3}{17}. \end{align}

This is not a constant, which means that $y = f(x)$ does not have a horizontal asymptote.

example.title: Finding a Horizontal Asymptote When the Degree of the Numerator is Greater

question.explanation:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to\infty.$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is $x^3.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by $x^3,$ as follows: \begin{align} f(x) & = \dfrac{7x^5 - 4x^3}{2x^3 + 9}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{7x^5}{x^3} - \dfrac{4x^3}{x^3}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{2x^3}{x^3} + \dfrac{9}{x^3} \right)}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\left(7x^2 - 4\right)}{\left(2 + \dfrac{9}{x^3} \right)} \end{align}

Now, when $x$ is very large, the term $\dfrac{9}{x^3}$ becomes very small. Therefore, as $x\to\infty,$ we have

\begin{align} f(x) & = \dfrac{\left(7x^2 - 4\right)}{\left(2 + \dfrac{9}{x^3} \right)}\\[5pt] & \approx \dfrac{7x^2 - 4}{2 + 0}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2}(7x^2 - 4). \end{align}

This is not a constant, which means that $y = f(x)$ does not have a horizontal asymptote.
